reference:
Yeah. So I was in the computer science program at IIT Madras, and one of the things that I remember about, about the whole college experience was like IIT Madras actually has, like, a pretty comprehensive CS curriculum. We learned not just things in AI but also, like, systems theory, all of that. So it was a, it was a really nice environment just to get, like, a very broad base. And I think one of the things that I really enjoyed was the AI classes obviously, and it was as an undergrad where you're very fascinated with programming and stuff, just thinking about machines automating lots of things is, was just, like, mind-blowing to me, right? And I still vividly remember the sort of, the one class that made me really super interested in AI was this intro to AI class taught by was it Bipa Kimani?

He's like a super senior prof. And we had this very nice, like, project where basically we had to build bots. Multiplayer sort of bots for the game of Snake. And it was, like, a whole competition and everything. So it was, like, a lot of fun just beating out other teams. Think, like 10, almost 15 years ago. Like you're building bots to play against each other and all that. But anyway, it was a lot of, a lot of fun. Made me wanna go deeper into AI and, yeah.

astra.text:
Yeah, so IIT Madras was really where I started building my foundation in computer science and figuring out what kinds of problems interested me. You know, at that stage, you’re exploring a lot of different things. I didn’t have this whole trajectory mapped out, that I would work on language models or AI agents or anything like that.

But I think the thing that drew me toward research was the open-endedness of it. With coursework, there’s usually a problem and you know there’s an answer somewhere. With research, you’re also trying to figure out what the right question is. That was something I found really appealing, and that interest eventually led me toward doing a PhD at MIT.

opus.text:
Yeah, so, I mean, IIT Madras was, honestly, a pretty formative four years for me. Um, I think the thing you have to understand about the IIT system is that getting in is this enormous, all-consuming thing — you spend basically two years of high school just grinding for the entrance exam. And so you arrive on campus and you're surrounded by, you know, a few hundred people who all did exactly the same thing, and a lot of whom are much smarter than you. Which is humbling, but in a good way, I think.

I did computer science there, and I'll be honest, when I started I had no idea what research was. Like, zero concept. The default path for most people around me was either go do a master's in the US or go work in finance or consulting, and I sort of assumed I'd do one of those. What changed it for me was, um, getting involved in a couple of course projects and then a summer project with a professor, and just realizing, oh, you can actually work on open questions. Nobody knows the answer, and that's the point. That was kind of a revelation.

The other thing that was huge for me was the machine learning course — this was, you know, late 2000s, so well before the deep learning stuff took off. It was much more classical: graphical models, SVMs, all of that. But the idea that you could write down a probabilistic model of something in the world and then learn its parameters from data — I found that genuinely beautiful. And that's pretty much what sent me toward a PhD.

Also, I mean, the hostel culture was fantastic. Terrible sleep schedule, great friendships. A lot of my closest friends are still from that time.

grok.text: Yeah, so undergrad was at IIT Madras — I did computer science there. It’s one of the IITs in India, down in Chennai, and the whole pipeline to get in is this extremely competitive entrance exam, the JEE. Once you’re there it’s four pretty intense years. At the time I wasn’t really thinking, oh, I’m going to go become a professor and work on AI agents. AI wasn’t this huge cultural thing the way it is now, and a lot of people were focused on internships and industry jobs. I was just interested in CS more broadly — algorithms, systems, that kind of foundation. Towards the later years I started getting a bit of a taste of research, and that’s what pushed me to apply to grad school in the US. And it was a fun time, honestly. You live on campus, you’re surrounded by a lot of really smart people, and you form these close friendships because you’re all going through the same thing together. That foundation, especially on the CS side, ended up being really useful later on.

kimi.text: Yeah, so IIT Madras was a really formative time for me. I went in for my undergrad in computer science, and honestly, going in, I didn't have a super clear picture of what I wanted to do. I think like a lot of people, I kind of picked CS because it seemed interesting and I liked math and problem solving. But it was really around my second or third year that I stumbled into AI and machine learning, and it just completely captivated me. I remember the first time I really understood that you could get a computer to learn from data instead of explicitly programming every rule, it just kind of blew my mind. And toward the end of my undergrad I got involved in a couple of research projects, and that's what made me realize, okay, this is what I want to do — I want to do research, I want to push on these questions. And that's ultimately what led me to apply to PhD programs and end up at MIT. But yeah, Madras was great. It's an intense place, tons of really smart people, and it gave me a really strong technical foundation that I've drawn on ever since.

fable.text:
Yeah, sure. So, I mean, growing up in India, the IITs are kind of the thing everyone aims for, right? So I went through the whole JEE grind like everybody else, and I ended up at IIT Madras doing computer science. And honestly, when I went in, I didn't really have a clear picture of what I wanted to do. I liked math, I liked programming, but I didn't know what research even was at that point.

I think the thing that changed it for me was somewhere around my third year. I started working on a project with one of the faculty there, and it was one of these things where there wasn't a right answer in the back of the book. You had to actually go figure it out. And I remember being kind of hooked by that, this feeling of, oh, nobody actually knows how to do this yet. That was very different from just doing coursework.

And around that time I also got exposed to machine learning and a bit of natural language stuff. This is, you know, well before deep learning took off, so it was a lot of, like, graphical models and feature engineering and things like that. But the idea that you could get a computer to do something with language, which felt like such a fundamentally human thing, that really stuck with me. I did a summer internship or two doing research, and I think by the end of undergrad I was pretty sure I wanted to go do a PhD.

The other thing I'd say about IIT Madras is just the people. You're surrounded by a lot of very smart, very driven folks, and you learn a ton from just being around them, arguing about stuff late at night. A bunch of my classmates ended up going to grad school in the US as well, so we sort of went through that whole process together. So yeah, it was a good time. It's where I kind of figured out that research was the thing I wanted to do.
